category_title: Children with communication difficulties and reactive behavioral outbursts
minimal_context: Angus is having a one-to-one conversation with his teacher to recount an incident that happened in the playground.
dialogue:
TUTOR: Angus, tell me what happened in the playground.

STUDENT: (Speaking very quickly and getting over-excited) They were over there and then... and then he came up and... it was just...

TUTOR: Keep going, what else happened?

STUDENT: I don't... wait. He took it and then... I don't know what I was saying! (Looks highly flustered)

TUTOR: Just try to explain it to me.

STUDENT: I can't! (Gets visibly annoyed, kicks the chair leg, and turns away, refusing to continue the conversation)

options.A: Explicitly teach that people can have the same facts but different perspectives; use variations in playground stories as a perfect example of this subjectivity.
options.B: Allow him time to recognize his over-excitement, stop, think about what he wanted to say about the playground incident, and start the conversation again.
options.C: Call to Angus and explain: 'This event, it's the first part, it's here [points to the table]. You must explain the next part that comes after.'
options.D: Use arms to block out the space of the playground, creating a visual of what the incident looked like and showing where the students were.
